claims.text: The initial material is a homogeneous, well-mixed, single-source mixture of noble-metal complexes at room temperature.
Intermittent isothermal holds enable controlled precursor conversion.
Intermittent isothermal holds regulate atomic mobility.
Controlled precursor conversion and atomic mobility synchronize nucleation among the alloy components.
Synchronized nucleation suppresses phase separation.
Suppression of phase separation promotes uniform, single-phase solid-solution noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
The intervention is a step-wise temperature ramp containing optimized isothermal holds at temperatures that activate precursor conversion while limiting excessive diffusion.
Maintaining moderate atomic diffusion during the plateaus prevents grain growth or sintering.
Isothermal holds permit gradual formation of metal atoms from the precursors.
Gradual metal-atom formation enables synchronized and homogeneous nucleation across all metal components.
Controlled diffusion prevents early-stage particle coalescence.
Controlled diffusion prevents elemental segregation.
Relative to continuous rapid heating, the step-wise profile will increase single-phase character.
Relative to continuous rapid heating, the step-wise profile will reduce elemental segregation.
Relative to continuous rapid heating, the step-wise profile will improve control of particle morphology.
Relative to continuous rapid heating, the step-wise profile will lower the effective thermal decomposition threshold.
Continuous rapid heating without intermittent holds typically produces phase separation, elemental segregation, and irregular morphology.
The hypothesis applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic noble-metal HEAs containing combinations of Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, Rh, and Ir under rapid-heating and rapid-cooling conditions.
Optimal hold temperatures and durations vary with precursor chemistry and nanoparticle scale.
Excessive diffusion during the holds may cause sintering and grain growth.
